findings.title: Routine, error-free cleanup operations logged at Error severity on every batch
findings.description: The new batched delete paths in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error unconditionally after every successful fetchIDs/deleteByIDs call, even when no error occurred and even when zero rows are found; the file's only other logging convention (line 410) uses log.Info for routine events. Combined with the cleanup ticker interval being cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute in the same PR, this floods logs with spurious ERROR-level entries on every tick for every configured annotation type, which can trigger false alerts/paging and drown out genuine errors.
findings.evidence: Line 534: r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) is reached only after `if err != nil { return 0, err }` at line 531-533, so `err` logged here is always nil; the same pattern repeats at 537 (message says "cleaned" but logs at Error level unconditionally), 554, 557, 576, 579. Pre-existing convention at line 410 uses r.log.Info("delete", "orgId", params.OrgID) for a comparable routine operation.
findings.suggestion: Use r.log.Debug or r.log.Info for the routine per-batch progress messages, and reserve r.log.Error for the branch where the returned error is actually non-nil (e.g. only log at Error level inside `if y != nil { ... }`).

findings.title: Cleanup ticker cut to 1 minute but per-cycle timeout left at 9 minutes
findings.description: The background cleanup ticker interval was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but the internal per-cycle deadline in clean() (const timeout = 9 * time.Minute, unchanged) still allows a single pass over all eight registered jobs to run up to 9x longer than the new tick interval. Since Run() calls srv.clean(ctx) synchronously inside the select loop, a slow pass (now more likely for annotation cleanup, whose delete path was changed in this PR from one atomic DELETE per type to many sequential fetch+delete round trips) will simply cause the next tick to fire immediately after the previous pass completes, collapsing the intended 1-minute cadence into near-continuous back-to-back execution of every registered cleanup job under load.
findings.evidence: Line 77: `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` (previously 10); line 89 (unchanged): `const timeout = 9 * time.Minute` inside clean(), which still bounds a single synchronous pass over cleanupJobs including cleanUpOldAnnotations.
findings.suggestion: Reduce the internal per-cycle timeout proportionally when reducing the ticker interval, or run clean() in a way that skips a tick if the previous pass is still in flight, to avoid an unbounded reduction in idle time between cleanup passes under load.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval cut from 10m to 1m ripples into 6 unrelated jobs and contradicts two docs pages
findings.description: The ticker driving CleanUpService.Run was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute; that same ticker fires clean(), which sequentially runs seven other jobs implemented in separate packages (temp file/image cleanup, dashboard snapshot expiry, dashboard version expiry, alert image expiry, user invite expiry, short URL cleanup, query history cleanup), none of which were touched or re-tested in this PR, so all now execute roughly ten times more often than before. Two documentation pages also assert the old 10-minute cadence for the same job.
findings.evidence: pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go:77 `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` (was `time.Minute * 10`); clean() at line 96-105 lists cleanupJobs across dashboardsnapshots, dashver, image, tempuser, shorturls and queryhistory packages; docs/sources/setup-grafana/image-rendering/_index.md:27 states "A background job runs every 10 minutes and removes temporary images"; docs/sources/dashboards/create-reports/index.md:136 states "A background job runs every 10 minutes and removes temporary CSV files" — both describing srv.cleanUpTmpFiles which is driven by this same ticker.
findings.suggestion: Either scope the faster cadence to only the annotation-cleanup job (e.g. run annotation cleanup on its own ticker/loop) or, if the global 1-minute cadence is intentional, update both documentation pages and verify the other six jobs (DB queries, image-store calls, file-system scans) tolerate a 10x increase in invocation frequency without added load or lock contention.

findings.title: Context-cancellation branch of the new untilDoneOrCancelled helper is never exercised
findings.description: The refactor extracted the retry loop into a standalone, DB-free function untilDoneOrCancelled(ctx, batchWork) shared by CleanAnnotations (both MaxAge and MaxCount paths) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags. Its ctx.Done() branch, which must stop the batch loop and return the correct partial totalAffected plus ctx.Err(), is not exercised by any test even though the function's decoupling from the DB session now makes it trivial to unit test with a cancelled context and a stub batchWork callback.
findings.evidence: xorm_store.go lines 645-659: `select { case <-ctx.Done(): return totalAffected, ctx.Err(); default: affected, err := batchWork(); totalAffected += affected; ... }`. Grep across pkg/services/annotations shows untilDoneOrCancelled is referenced only at its call sites (lines 528, 548, 570) and its own definition; cleanup_test.go and xorm_store_test.go only run the fully successful path against a live SQLite DB via db.InitTestDB and never pass a cancelled/expired context into CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags/CleanAnnotations.
findings.suggestion: Add a small, DB-free unit test that calls untilDoneOrCancelled directly (or via CleanAnnotations with a context.WithCancel context cancelled before/while the callback runs) with a stub batchWork that counts invocations, asserting the returned error is the context's error and that totalAffected reflects only batches completed before cancellation.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that drops the ctx.Err() return, or reorders the accumulation so totalAffected is discarded on cancellation, would let the cleanup loop keep running (or silently report zero progress) past a caller-cancelled or timed-out context, and no existing test would fail because cancellation is never exercised.

findings.title: No test covers deleteByIDs failing (or affecting 0 rows) after fetchIDs already returned ids
findings.description: This PR replaced a single atomic DELETE...WHERE id IN (subquery) statement with two separate DB round-trips, fetchIDs (SELECT) then deleteByIDs (DELETE), introducing a new window where the delete step can fail or affect fewer rows than fetchIDs found (e.g. a concurrent delete or a DB error between the two calls). Every test in this PR only exercises the fully-successful pairing against a live, healthy SQLite database, so the error-propagation and premature-loop-termination behavior of this new two-phase design is unverified.
findings.evidence: xorm_store.go lines 530-538: `ids, err := r.fetchIDs(ctx, "annotation", cond); ... x, y := r.deleteByIDs(ctx, "annotation", ids); ... return x, y` feeding into untilDoneOrCancelled's `if affected == 0 { return totalAffected, nil }` at line 656 — if deleteByIDs affects 0 rows despite ids being non-empty (e.g. concurrently deleted rows), the loop stops even though further batches may remain. cleanup_test.go's TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp and TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst only run against db.InitTestDB with no induced failure between the SELECT and DELETE steps.
findings.suggestion: Extend pkg/infra/db/dbtest.FakeDB (or add a small custom db.DB stub) so a callback can succeed on the first WithDbSession call (populating ids) and fail on the second, then add a unit test asserting CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags propagates the delete error and reports the correct partial totalAffected rather than swallowing it or looping forever.
findings.failure_scenario: If a future change drops the `if err != nil { return x, err }`-equivalent propagation from deleteByIDs's result, or the loop's zero-affected short-circuit masks a real DB error as "done", annotations logged as "to clean" would never actually be deleted (or the job would silently under-report), and no current test would detect it.

findings.title: New cleanup logging uses Error level for routine successful operations, not actual errors
findings.description: Six new log calls in the batched cleanup helpers use r.log.Error to report routine counts ("Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by count", "Tags to clean", etc.) even on the success path where the preceding err check has already returned early on failure, so err is guaranteed nil at the call site; this contradicts both the Logger interface's documented Error contract and the file's own pre-existing precedent of using Info for routine operations, and will emit Error-level log lines on every successful cleanup cycle, which now runs every minute after the cleanup.go ticker change.
findings.evidence: xorm_store.go:534,537,554,557,576,579 all call r.log.Error(...) unconditionally for success-path reporting; by contrast the pre-existing line 410 in the same file uses r.log.Info("delete", "orgId", params.OrgID) for an analogous routine operation; pkg/infra/log/interface.go:30 documents "// Error logs a message with error level and key/value pairs, if any."
findings.suggestion: Use r.log.Info (or r.log.Debug) for the routine "found N to clean"/"cleaned N" messages, reserving r.log.Error for the actual error branches (which already return early via `if err != nil`).
findings.claude_md_rule: pkg/infra/log/interface.go:30 — "// Error logs a message with error level and key/value pairs, if any." combined with the file's own established precedent at xorm_store.go:410 (`r.log.Info("delete", "orgId", params.OrgID)`) of using Info for routine, non-error operations.

findings.title: New integration-test skip message capitalized inconsistently with documented example and existing package usage
findings.description: The two newly-added integration test skip checks use t.Skip("Skipping integration test") with a capital S, while the backend style guide's documented example and every other short-skip call in this same package use a lowercase "skipping integration test"; this is a small but real inconsistency introduced by this diff (the two calls did not exist before this change).
findings.evidence: cleanup_test.go:20 and :153 use t.Skip("Skipping integration test"); grep across the package shows annotations_test.go:36, annotations_test.go:178, xorm_store_test.go:30 and accesscontrol_test.go:20 all use the lowercase form matching contribute/backend/style-guide.md's example `t.Skip("skipping integration test")`.
findings.suggestion: Lowercase the 's' to match the style guide's example and the rest of the package: t.Skip("skipping integration test").
findings.claude_md_rule: contribute/backend/style-guide.md lines 38-44: the documented integration-test template shows `t.Skip("skipping integration test")` (lowercase), and the rest of the package follows that exact casing.

findings.title: Fetch-log-delete-log pattern duplicated three times in xorm_store.go
findings.description: The closure passed to untilDoneOrCancelled in the MaxAge branch (lines 528-539), the MaxCount branch (548-559), and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (570-581) all follow the identical sequence: build a condition string, call r.fetchIDs, log the fetch, call r.deleteByIDs, log the delete, and return the pair. Only the table name, the WHERE condition, and the two log message strings differ between the three copies, so a future change to the fetch/delete/log sequence (e.g. adding a metric, changing error handling) has to be made in three places and can easily drift.
findings.evidence: Lines 528-539 (annotation by time), 548-559 (annotation by count), and 570-581 (annotation_tag) each contain: ids, err := r.fetchIDs(...); if err != nil { return 0, err }; r.log.Error(beforeMsg, ...); x, y := r.deleteByIDs(...); r.log.Error(afterMsg, ...); return x, y.
findings.suggestion: Extract a shared helper, e.g. func (r *xormRepositoryImpl) fetchAndDeleteBatch(ctx context.Context, table, cond, beforeMsg, afterMsg string) (int64, error) { ids, err := r.fetchIDs(ctx, table, cond); if err != nil { return 0, err }; r.log.Error(beforeMsg, "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err); affected, err := r.deleteByIDs(ctx, table, ids); r.log.Error(afterMsg, "count", len(ids), "affected", affected, "err", err); return affected, err }. Each of the three call sites then becomes: return untilDoneOrCancelled(ctx, func() (int64, error) { cond := fmt.Sprintf(...); return r.fetchAndDeleteBatch(ctx, "annotation", cond, "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time") }), passing the exact original message strings so log output is unchanged.
findings.behavior_preserved: Yes, if the exact original log message strings and field order are passed through as parameters to the shared helper, the observable log output, return values, and error propagation are unchanged.

findings.title: Log call includes an 'err' field that is always nil
findings.description: In all three fetch/delete blocks, the pre-delete log call includes an 'err' keyed field sourced from the same err variable that was just checked non-nil and returned on two lines earlier, so the value logged here is always nil. Logging a field that can never be anything but nil (at Error level, no less) is misleading to a reader debugging from logs and adds noise without information.
findings.evidence: Line 534: r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) immediately follows the guard at lines 531-533 (if err != nil { return 0, err }), so err is guaranteed nil at line 534; the same pattern repeats at line 554 and line 576.
findings.suggestion: Drop the always-nil "err", err key/value pair from the pre-delete log calls, e.g. change r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) to r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond).
findings.behavior_preserved: Yes, removing a field whose value is provably always nil does not change any conditional logic, return value, or error path.

findings.title: Single-letter variable names x, y obscure what deleteByIDs returns
findings.description: The results of r.deleteByIDs are bound to x and y at all three call sites, then immediately used in a log call and a return statement. The values are the affected-row count and an error, which is exactly what descriptive names like affected and err would say directly; x and y force the reader to trace back to the callee signature to know what is being logged and returned.
findings.evidence: Line 536: x, y := r.deleteByIDs(ctx, "annotation", ids) followed by line 537: r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y) and line 538: return x, y; the same x, y pattern recurs at lines 556-558 and 578-580.
findings.suggestion: Rename x, y to affected, err at all three sites, e.g. change x, y := r.deleteByIDs(ctx, "annotation", ids) to affected, err := r.deleteByIDs(ctx, "annotation", ids), and update the following log/return lines to use affected and err.
findings.behavior_preserved: Yes, this is a pure rename with no logic change; err shadows the already-checked outer err from fetchIDs within the same closure scope, which is legal and does not affect control flow.

findings.title: Batch-insert loop duplicated for annotations and annotation tags
findings.description: createTestAnnotations runs the same batch-insert loop twice, once over newAnnotations and once over newAnnotationTags, differing only in the slice being inserted; the loop body (compute the batch bound with min, call sess.InsertMulti, assert no error) is copy-pasted rather than shared, so a future change to batching (e.g. a different batch size or added retry) has to be made twice.
findings.evidence: Lines 273-281 insert newAnnotations in batches of 500 via sess.InsertMulti(newAnnotations[i:min(i+batchsize, len(newAnnotations))]); lines 283-291 repeat the identical loop structure for newAnnotationTags.
findings.suggestion: Extract a small generic helper, e.g. func insertBatched[T any](t *testing.T, sess *db.Session, items []T, batchSize int) { for i := 0; i < len(items); i += batchSize { _, err := sess.InsertMulti(items[i:min(i+batchSize, len(items))]); require.NoError(t, err) } }, then call insertBatched(t, sess, newAnnotations, 500) and insertBatched(t, sess, newAnnotationTags, 500) inside the two WithDbSession callbacks.
findings.behavior_preserved: Yes, the insert order, batch size, and error assertions are identical; only the duplicated loop body is consolidated.
